grammar.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
grammar.explanation:
Use the **past simple** for a time that is finished. The action ended, and we often say when it happened: yesterday, last week, or in 2019.

Use the **present perfect** when the past connects to now. The time is not finished, or the exact time is not important.

The **past simple** form is the second form of the verb: **went**, **had**, **broke**. For questions and negatives, use **did**: **Did** you **work**?

The **present perfect** form is **have** or **has** plus the past participle: I **have worked**, she **has gone**.

Use the **present perfect** for life experience with no time given. *Have you ever been to Japan?* asks about your life up to now.

Use the **present perfect** with **since** and **for** for a period that continues until now. Our carpenter **has worked** with wood **since** 2019, and he still loves the job.

Use the **past simple** for a finished period. A builder who **lived** in Italy for ten years does not live there now.

Never use the **present perfect** with a finished time word. Say *I **saw** the CEO yesterday*, never *I have seen the CEO yesterday*.

Questions with **When** always use the **past simple**: **When did** the truck break down? **When did** Sara start her job?

practice.q: Rewrite with the past simple: Sara has started her new job yesterday.
practice.a: Sara started her new job yesterday.

practice.q: Rewrite with the present perfect: Tom worked as a carpenter since 2019. (He still works there.)
practice.a: Tom has worked as a carpenter since 2019.

practice.q: Rewrite with the past simple: The CEO has visited the building site last week.
practice.a: The CEO visited the building site last week.

practice.q: Rewrite with the present perfect: I build brick houses for ten years. (I still build them.)
practice.a: I have built brick houses for ten years.
